statements.quote: We speak of "the information age" as if information became valuable only recently.
Information has been a **commodity** — something produced, shipped, priced, and traded — for centuries.
But a commodity is not just "valuable things"; a commodity is valuable *because it moves*.
It has producers, a price, a channel, and buyers.

So the question this chapter asks is not "when did information become important?" but **how was a *market* for it built** — because a market, with a flow, is the thing everything after it (the encyclopedia, the database, the web) runs on.
The first layer is the **market** itself.

A letter describing a significant event was copied and circulated as a news report; and a common device was a plain listing of current prices, the circulation of which quickened international trade \cite[News — early news networks, Wikipedia]{fuggernews}.

blocks.section: The coffee-house public sphere

blocks.quote: A commodity needs a **public**. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the venue was the coffee house. The sociologist \citeauthor{habermaspublicsphere} (\citeyear{habermaspublicsphere}) later named what was happening there: the **public sphere** — a space that was physically a coffee house in Britain, a salon in France, a reading society in Germany, where private individuals gathered to talk about *printed matter* as a shared reality \cite[the coffee-house public sphere, Habermas]{habermaspublicsphere}.
blocks.section: The coffee-house public sphere

blocks.quote: Notice what is new. The authority is not in any single person's rank, title, or lineage. It is in the **forum**: you argued a point, but you argued it to a public that had *read the same paper*. Information stopped being a private possession in the head of the Fugger banker and became the raw material of a collective, argument-generating public. The news sheet (the commodity) and the coffee house (the venue) are two halves of the same invention: a way for a *society* to share and contest what it knows.

blocks.quote: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville
blocks.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

blocks.quote: The urge to gather *all* knowledge into one place is far older than the Enlightenment. Nearly eleven centuries before Diderot, in Visigothic Spain, the archbishop \cite[Isidore of Seville]{isidoreofseville} (c. 560–636) compiled the *\citetitle{etymologiae}* — a twenty-book encyclopedia that tried to capture the whole of ancient learning in a single ordered work. Its modern translators call it "arguably the most influential book, after the Bible, in the learned world of the Latin West for nearly a thousand years" \cite{etymologiae}.
blocks.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

blocks.quote: Isidore did not merely store the classics; he reorganized them. Drawing on hundreds of earlier authors — Pliny, Solinus, Servius, the church fathers — he sorted everything from grammar, rhetoric, and the mathematical *quadrivium* to medicine, law, animals, geography, and the making of furniture into twenty books, each a folder in one universal filing cabinet \cite{etymologiae}. The *Etymologiae* became *the* textbook of the Middle Ages, copied in nearly a thousand surviving manuscripts; so completely did it stand in for the originals that some classical works stopped being copied and were lost, surviving only as his excerpts \cite{etymologiae}.
blocks.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

blocks.quote: It is a fitting accident of history, then, that the Catholic Church has come to regard Isidore as the patron saint of the internet — and of computer users and programmers. The identification is best described as a popular, informal patronage: in the early 2000s Catholic internet groups and a Vatican media office promoted Isidore for the role, but no formal papal decree is documented, which is itself a very Isidorean sort of uncertainty (\cite[Shachtman, 2002]{wired2002isidore}). A seventh-century bishop who tried to put the whole world into twenty books is, at the very least, the right ancestor for the thing this chapter is about.
blocks.section: Before the Encyclopédie: Isidore of Seville

blocks.quote: The Encyclopédie and the Mundaneum
blocks.section: The Encyclopédie and the Mundaneum

blocks.quote: The Encyclopédie: compiling everything at once
blocks.section: The Encyclopédie: compiling everything at once

blocks.quote: If the coffee house was where information was *discussed*, the Encyclopédie was the great eighteenth-century attempt to **collect** it. Between 1751 and 1772, \citeauthor{encyclopedie} and some hundred and forty contributors set out to put *all* known knowledge into a single work — the sciences, the arts, the trades — and, crucially, to **cross-reference** the articles to one another: a device the history of the book calls "a kind of precursor to the hyperlink" \cite[the Encyclopédie, Diderot & d'Alembert]{encyclopedie}.
blocks.section: The Encyclopédie: compiling everything at once

blocks.quote: The ambition was not merely to *store* knowledge but to *connect* it — and in doing so, to change how people thought. This is the **corpus** in its first systematic form: a body of text, organized and internally linked, large enough that it becomes an object in its own right. You can now point at "the Encyclopédie" the way you later point at "the web" — as a single, structured, interlinked thing. Two centuries after Diderot, that object has a new name: the *training corpus* \cite[the Encyclopédie, Diderot & d'Alembert]{encyclopedie}.

blocks.quote: Paul Otlet and the Mundaneum: the library that wanted to be the world
blocks.section: Paul Otlet and the Mundaneum: the library that wanted to be the world

blocks.quote: The final layer is the one that was missing from the story for a hundred years, because it was almost lost. In 1910 two Belgian lawyers — \cite[Paul Otlet]{paulotlet} and Henri La Fontaine — built the **Mundaneum** in Brussels \cite[the Mundaneum, Wikipedia]{mundaneum}. It was a *documentation of the world*: every book, article, and fact they could collect reduced to a standardized index card, classified by the Universal Decimal Classification and **cross-indexed**, so that a single fact sat in many drawers at once. At its height the building held more than twelve million cards — a physical model of the whole of human knowledge, *networked by index* \cite[the Mundaneum, Wikipedia]{mundaneum}.
blocks.section: Paul Otlet and the Mundaneum: the library that wanted to be the world

blocks.quote: 1934: the paper internet
blocks.section: 1934: the paper internet

blocks.quote: In 1934 Otlet published the \cite[Traité de Documentation]{traitededocumentation}, and with it the vision that the next forty years would chase. He described a network of what he called "electric telescopes" — a *worldwide network* (a *réseau mondial*) of interlinked documents, held in a central repository, that anyone could consult from their own armchair: a moving image of the world, projected on a personal screen \cite[Wright, Cataloging the World (2014)]{catalogingtheworld}. He called that central repository the **mundotheque** — his word for a "world-library" that would display any document on demand, from anywhere \cite[the Mundaneum, Wikipedia]{mundaneum}.
blocks.section: 1934: the paper internet

blocks.quote: Read that again: a network of linked documents, *retrievable by query, from a distance, on demand*. In 1934, with paper cards and telegraph lines, Otlet was describing a **paper internet** — before the word "internet" was ever applied to a network of computers. His 1934 vision directly prefigured the *Memex* that Vannevar Bush would make famous a decade later, and the [World Wide Web](untold_history_iii.php) that came after that. This is the hinge the course has been building toward: the moment the *corpus* stops being a thing you read in a room and becomes a thing you **query from anywhere**.
